title: SEWA: Organizing Women in the Informal Economy
summary: Founded in 1972 by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad, the Self-Employed Women's Association grew into India's largest single trade union — more than two million informal women workers — by pairing union organizing with cooperatives, its own bank, insurance, and childcare, and reframing street vendors and home-based workers as workers with rights.

keyData.label: Influence
keyData.value: Shaped WIEGO and global informal-work policy

content:
## Background

The overwhelming majority of India's workers — and of women workers in particular — earn their living in the informal economy: as street vendors, home-based garment stitchers, rag-pickers, head-loaders, bidi-rollers, and small farmers. For most of the twentieth century these workers were invisible to labour law and economic policy. Because they had no formal employer, they were not "workers" in the legal sense; because they were poor and often illiterate women, they had little bargaining power against wholesalers, moneylenders, municipal police, and landlords.

In Ahmedabad, a lawyer named Ela Bhatt worked in the women's wing of the Textile Labour Association, the union founded in the tradition of Gandhi. Encountering the head-loaders and used-garment dealers who worked around the mills, she saw workers with all the vulnerability of employment and none of its protections. In 1972 she helped found the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA) as a trade union of poor, self-employed women.

## The Intervention

SEWA's founding insight was that poor women needed both **struggle and development** — the confrontational tools of a union and the constructive tools of cooperatives and finance. Registering informal workers as a union was itself a battle: authorities objected that women without a formal employer could not unionize. SEWA prevailed, establishing that self-employed workers have collective rights.

Around the union SEWA built an ecosystem of member-owned institutions. In 1974, after members complained that banks would not serve them and moneylenders charged ruinous rates, SEWA founded its own cooperative bank, the SEWA Bank, capitalized by members' own shares. Over the following decades it added dozens of cooperatives (of artisans, vendors, dairy producers, and service providers), a member-based insurance arm (VimoSEWA), childcare cooperatives, health workers, and legal aid. Members paid dues and owned the institutions; SEWA organized rather than delivered charity.

The organization also became a policy actor, campaigning for legal recognition of street vendors and home-based workers, contributing to national vendor legislation and to international labour standards on home work.

## Results & Evidence

SEWA's most unambiguous achievement is its scale and durability. From a few thousand members it grew to more than two million women across several Indian states, making it the largest single primary trade union in India and one of the largest organizations of informal workers in the world. That it has survived and expanded for half a century, remaining member-financed and member-governed, is itself strong evidence that the model is viable.

Evaluations of SEWA's component programmes are more mixed and mostly observational rather than experimental. Studies of SEWA Bank document improved access to savings and credit and reduced dependence on moneylenders, though impacts on income are harder to isolate. Research on VimoSEWA highlights both the value and the difficulty of sustaining voluntary micro-insurance among very poor members. Analyses of SEWA's organizing consistently emphasize gains that are hard to quantify but repeatedly reported: higher and steadier earnings from collective bargaining with contractors, protection from harassment and eviction, financial literacy, and — members themselves stress this — a sense of identity and voice.

Perhaps SEWA's largest measurable impact is on ideas and institutions. It co-founded WIEGO (Women in Informal Employment: Globalizing and Organizing), which reshaped how statisticians and policymakers count and think about informal work, and its model has been studied and adapted by organizations of informal workers across Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

## Challenges & Criticisms

SEWA's strengths are also its constraints. A model built on patient organizing and member ownership is hard to scale quickly or to replicate by decree; much of SEWA's success rests on decades of trust-building and on exceptional leadership, which are not easily transplanted. The very poor sometimes struggle to sustain dues, savings, or insurance premiums, and voluntary schemes face adverse selection and lapses.

Because SEWA is simultaneously a union, a federation of cooperatives, and a financial institution, rigorous causal evaluation of "SEWA" as a whole is nearly impossible; the evidence base is rich in description and case study but thin in experimental identification. Critics also note that organizing cannot substitute for the structural policies — social protection, urban planning, macroeconomic demand — that ultimately shape the informal economy.

## Key Lessons

- **Informal workers can be organized.** SEWA disproved the assumption that workers without a formal employer cannot unionize, expanding the very definition of a worker.
- **Struggle plus development.** Combining bargaining power with member-owned finance and services proved more durable than either organizing or microfinance alone.
- **Member ownership builds durability.** Financing institutions through members' own dues and shares, rather than external grants, aligned incentives and produced a fifty-year organization.
- **Impact runs through ideas.** SEWA's reframing of informal work — institutionalized through WIEGO — changed statistics and policy far beyond its own membership.
- **Not everything that matters is measurable.** Voice, dignity, and security are central to what members value and to why the model persists, even where income effects are hard to identify.
